item.title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index
item.abstract: Google DeepMind just released Gemini 4 Neon . Gemini 4 Neon is a reasoning model that sits between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It targets coding agents, knowledge work and science workflows. The developer pitch is near-frontier scores at a lower cost per task. Pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. Neon is the middle model in the Gemini 4 family. Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon projects. Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon balances depth and efficiency between the two. As per the model card , Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count or architecture. Inputs cover text, images, audio and video. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Neon exposes multiple thinking levels. High is the default. xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and makes fewer redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity , Neon can act as an orchestrator. It directs parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller subtasks. Google compares Neon against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. All scores below are reported by Google, not independently reproduced. Neon does not win every row. Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (47.3% vs 46.2%). GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography (75.1% vs 73.5%). On the Vals Index , Neon scores 70.9% and ranks #2. On the Agent Arena index it also ranks #2, with a score of 1336. Neon lists at $3 input, $0.15 cached input and $15 output per 1M tokens. Google says Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It also claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task vs rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. Those are per-task claims, not per-token prices. GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10. Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. Gemini 4 Carbon is $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20. Neon runs on the Gemini 4 safety and security stack . Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite. It passes 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation. It shows a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its 2.45% shortcut rate on a coding cheating test is the lowest of any Gemini 4 model. *Scores from Google’s launch comparison table , self-reported. AA scores for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol match Artificial Analysis . Check out the launch post and the model card . item.title: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo
item.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks more successfully. Inference drives this process. Workers generate rollouts: sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions. The RL framework scores the results, updates model weights, and sends those weights back to the workers for the next round. As RL training scales, redundant compute work, slow rollouts, weight updates, and worker failures can waste GPU capacity and delay training. NVIDIA Dynamo provides the serving layer to address these constraints, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster. This blog post explains the rollout bottlenecks that slow RL training and how Dynamo addresses them through routing, ModelExpress weight updates, and recovery. Figure 1. The RL loop generates rollouts, assigns rewards, and updates model weights before repeating 1. Why RL needs distributed rollout infrastructure A reasoning rollout may contain one response. A coding-agent rollout can involve repository exploration, edits, tool calls, and tests. These differences create an uneven workload across inference workers. Three constraints determine how effectively that workload supports training. Rollout completion time. When training requires a group of samples, the slowest required rollout can delay the next step. Distributing request counts evenly across GPUs does not necessarily distribute work evenly. Repeated context. Multiple attempts often begin with identical instructions, task descriptions, or coding repository context. Recomputing those prefixes consumes GPU capacity before new output is generated. Weight freshness. Training produces new model weights throughout the run. Workers must receive them according to the algorithm’s requirements for sampling and acceptable staleness. Addressing these constraints can let teams complete more iterations within a fixed compute budget. The right optimization depends on which constraint limits the workload. Figure 2. The three constraints on RL training: slow rollouts, redundant prompt processing, and timely weight updates 2. The Dynamo architecture for RL Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers. The RL framework submits generation requests; Dynamo routes them to eligible capacity; inference engines execute the model. Figure 3. Dynamo coordinates rollout serving, the RL framework controls training and ModelExpress distributes weights The responsibilities of each component remain explicit: Component Role RL framework Optimization, rewards, environments, checkpoints, and sample acceptance Dynamo Routing, worker management, serving controls, and telemetry Inference engine Generation and application of updated weights ModelExpress Model-weight and artifact distribution through supported integrations Table 1. Component responsibilities in the Dynamo RL training loop The generation and weight administration follow distinct paths. Requests use the shared serving frontend, while refresh operations target selected workers under framework control. This lets the framework determine when workers may generate samples and which results are eligible for training. The separation allows teams to improve serving without transferring ownership of the learning process. Routing decisions determine where generation runs; the framework determines whether the resulting samples satisfy its training requirements. See the RL integration reference . 3. How Dynamo accelerates routing, weight distribution, and recovery KV-aware routing: Reduce repeated prompt computation RL often generates several solutions to the same task using a shared prompt. Sending these requests to a worker that has cached the prompt avoids repeated processing, saving GPU compute. But sending every request to that worker can create a queue, delaying rollouts and the next training step. Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant computation and waiting. The objective is earlier completion of the samples needed for training. Figure 4. Dynamo balances cache reuse and worker load to reduce rollout delays ModelExpress: Reduce recurring weight-distribution overhead RL training repeatedly updates the model. Sending a full checkpoint to every rollout worker takes time and can interrupt generation. ModelExpress reduces this overhead by reusing weights already available in the cluster instead of loading from remote storage. Compatible workers can copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL. Figure 5. ModelExpress loads weights from a running worker’s GPU memory, making them available sooner than loading from storage Delta weight transfer reduces the data sent between updates. Instead of moving the full model, it sends a compressed representation of what changed. Workers reconstruct the new weights from the matching base version, reducing transfer time and network traffic. This also helps recovery. A replacement worker can load a checkpoint and apply subsequent deltas to catch up with the training run. Healthy workers can continue generating rollouts while capacity is restored. Figure 6. ModelExpress accelerates weight updates by transferring compressed changes instead of the full model The RL framework coordinates when workers apply updates, handles cached state, and checks readiness before accepting new samples. Recovery: Limit the impact of worker failures Long training runs must accommodate worker failures without unnecessarily interrupting healthy capacity. Dynamo detects worker loss, directs new requests toward eligible workers and adds replacement workers to routing once ready, keeping rollout generation moving when a worker fails. Supported configurations also enable migration for eligible in-flight requests and graceful draining. The RL framework handles interrupted samples and ensures replacements use the required weights. Figure 7. Dynamo reroutes supported sessions to healthy workers, using saved history to avoid restarting the full rollout Dynamo in RL workflows Dynamo adoption in RL spans frontier-model development, managed infrastructure and open source frameworks: Microsoft AI used NVIDIA Dynamo to support RL rollout inference during post-training . CoreWeave uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates by up to 15×. Cognition used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7 . Prime Intellect uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration . H Company used Dynamo and ModelExpress to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%. Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks, including verl , NeMo RL , Slime , and prime-rl . Get started with Dynamo for RL Efficient RL infrastructure keeps rollout generation, weight distribution, and worker recovery moving together. Dynamo brings these serving capabilities into the training loop, helping teams turn distributed GPU capacity into accepted training samples and faster iterations. Explore the Dynamo RL documentation and start scaling the inference behind your next model. item.title: Gemini 4 Neon
item.abstract:
Introducing Gemini 4 Neon Nov 18, 2026 | Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google In this article Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior.

item.title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench
item.abstract: Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. Harness-Zero is the closest match, but it uses a separate agent to correct the student. Self-Improving Memory skips that step. item.title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips
item.abstract: At Exa , we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware ( AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2 ), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization. Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving. Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database. Our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices. Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill The preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the new model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices. AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance ( inf2.xlarge ), with one chip and two NeuronCores . Our workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so we run Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving us container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. The same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Our initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model. From that baseline, it became a march to push throughput (docs/sec) as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. The following chart shows the throughput gains at each milestone. Figure 3: Throughput improvement across optimization milestones Starting from the naive compile, a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement. The first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. We also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. The downcast outputs met our correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference (see Agentic methodology ), so the accuracy impact was within our acceptance threshold. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. These pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and we used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. A drop-in attention kernel gave us the next bump in performance. The next bottleneck was memory spill. Profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Using a drop-in MLP kernel as a steppingstone to profile the shortcomings of the pre-built implementation, we wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls. We used the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops, and memory operations, and only dropped into the lower-level NKI ISA for specific tensor operations. Keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers, and easier to debug. At this point we hit a wall. Per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what we saw with both cores running simultaneously. That gap meant our theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above our realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores. Profiling and experimentation showed that our workload wasn’t yet saturating the Tensor Engine. The remaining headroom was ours to claim by making the computation leaner. The clearest path left was to reduce the overall FLOPS needed to produce our results by eliminating waste. We rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in our model to cut FLOPS spent on padding. This is where kernel customization really paid off. Generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they can’t take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. We wrung more performance out of attention by tailoring the implementation to the real shape of our model’s head architecture. We also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. That cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup. In total, our final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against our initial baseline. Agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction. Using Flyte , an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. The workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. It then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware. The harness supports agents at different costs. Lightweight models handle tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters, and correctness checks prevent drift. Reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them. Matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Because many agents don’t know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped. So far, we have optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region ( us-west-2 ), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service. Exa schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Our scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts.

item.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
item.abstract:
I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it. Set Up Tools which I mostly use are these: TOOL use DeepSeek Harness + Deepseek v4.1 Flash Thats the AI I am using. Occasionaly I use Codex with Luna or Terra but Deepseek is super performant, fast and cheap Ghidra + MCP bridge The best in the market, free, disassembler and decompiler. With the MCP bridge agents can use it very well radare2 and kuna CLI disassemblers and decompilers. Not as good as Ghidra but much faster and possibly better usable for AIs Process What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this. Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions). Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later. Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image. Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better. On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do: Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings. Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature. Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware. Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead. Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have. SKILLS Here are some of my major skills I use frequently. Matt Pottock - Grill me It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt: text Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions
whose answers are crucial for your further progress.
Ask only one question at a time. mattpocock / skills Shell Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. Ghidra / other RE tooling skill It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation. ioma8 / ghidra-decompile-skill Java Agent skill + 22 Ghidra scripts for fast targeted decompilation, and the fix for GhidraMCP extension/Ghidra version mismatches. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. Hypothesis debugging That is also my own skill. Its related to how I wrote earlier how important it is to make the agent document everything into MD files. This skill forces agent who is getting stuck to follow this loop: Make a hypothesis of why / how something works. Write it down into CSV table of hypotheses, saved on disc. item.title: DaisyRose-27B
item.abstract:
All posts Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. We are releasing BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget. DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1 . The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes. High-quality Training Data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria. Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from. Every task is a long job with several problems chained together. Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens. There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time. Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory. 80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes. Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face , and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles . DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai . We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩

item.title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
item.abstract: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points: At each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens. The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document. Four properties matter in production: The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes. The following diagram shows how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools. Figure 1: Reference architecture. The numbered steps match the following flow. The agent runs on AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda. This is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does. Figure 2: Shield the tool. The customer name is replaced with a vault token before the search provider sees the query, and restored before the agent reads the results. This is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place. Figure 3: Shield the model. The interceptor de-identifies the prompt and the conversation history before the model reads them, and restores the tokens it minted for that call before the agent reads the answer. This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy. Figure 4: Shield the document. The interceptor checks the presigned URL against the allowlist and size limit, Skyflow Detect fetches and de-identifies the file, and the agent receives a link to the clean copy. Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives: Figure 5: The case note as stored (left) and the de-identified copy the agent receives (right). A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse. The following video shows Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original. Video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy. The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide: The Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace . To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run: The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models . Agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code.

item.title: Build Tool-Calling Parsers in Rust with AI Agents
item.abstract:
A tool call can arrive in pieces, an argument can be cut short, or model-specific markup can leak into the answer. A frontend parser turns that output, received as token IDs or decoded text, into visible text, reasoning, and tool calls an application can use. In this post, you’ll learn how tool-call parsing works and use an AI agent to build a parser for a new model. You’ll start with a weather request and a human-reviewed test set, using frontend-crates , the reusable Rust components behind NVIDIA Dynamo tool-calling parsers. Suppose you ask for the weather in Paris. The model may generate reasoning followed by a get_weather call with a city argument. The frontend prepares and tokenizes the prompt, then an inference engine runs the LLM to generate tokens. The parser consumes token IDs or decoded text and separates reasoning, visible text, and tool calls in order. A protocol adapter turns those events into an OpenAI-compatible response, using the same parsing path for batch JSON and streaming updates. Figure 1. The LLM generates tokens; the parser accepts token IDs or decoded text before response shaping The tricky part is recognizing where each piece starts and ends. A call can be malformed or incomplete, a marker can appear inside an argument, or ordinary text can surround the call. The parser has to handle these boundaries without losing data, duplicating calls, or leaking model-specific markup. Returning to the weather request: the model might stop halfway through a city name or call a tool that wasn’t offered. Either can disrupt the agent’s next action. The following NVIDIA Nemotron examples show these two failures. Syntax error. The argument and tool-call frame never close, so no complete call can be parsed. </think><tool_call>
<function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par Semantic error. The frame is valid, but the named tool is absent from the request. </think><tool_call>
<function=unknown_tool><parameter=city>Paris</parameter></function>
</tool_call> These failures require different handling. If the model names an unavailable tool, the parser reports the call it received, and the serving layer validates tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy. Changing the tool name would hide what the model actually generated. An incomplete call is harder to judge while the stream is open. The rest of the city name may arrive in the next chunk, and a marker can split across chunks, too. Emit too early and syntax leaks into the answer; wait too long and ordinary text gets delayed. The parser needs consistent rules for what to emit, what to buffer, and how to handle the end of the stream. A parser can encounter an unbounded range of inputs. With invalid input, it must follow documented recovery rules rather than guess the model’s intent. Even a syntactically valid call that conforms to the schema can be the wrong choice for the user’s request. The parser needs a consistent grammar and recovery policy so it can preserve valid data without inventing calls or leaking model-specific markup. To check those decisions, frontend-crates pairs model outputs with expected results in a shared Conformance Corpus. Using the Conformance Corpus Use the Conformance Corpus to check how applicable parsers handle behavior first observed in one model. Its language-neutral YAML fixtures pair fixed input with expected output, so Rust parsers and Python references can run the same cases. A regression test for leaked markup, duplicate calls, or lost arguments can cover other families when adapted to their grammars. For a new parser, start with all UNIFIED.* cases across model families. They cover complete, malformed, truncated, multiple, and interleaved calls, plus streaming boundaries and end-of-input behavior. Adapt inputs to your model’s grammar and request settings, add model-specific edge cases, and explain exclusions. You can’t test every possible output, but you can reuse cases from other formats. Table 1 shows the UNIFIED.1-tool_only case from the Parser Conformance Table . In this example, the GOLDEN test set pairs four model-specific inputs with the same expected result: get_weather with city set to Paris. The markers differ, but each case tests the same behavior. Adapting the input format makes the same behavioral test reusable across models. Model Native input Beam <|start|> assistant to=get_weather <|channel|> analysis <|constrain|> xml <|message|> <rfl:parameter name="city"> Paris </rfl:parameter> <|call|> GPT-OSS <|start|> assistant <|channel|> commentary to=functions.get_weather <|constrain|> json <|message|> {"city": "Paris"} <|call|> Muse Spark <|start|> assistant to=get_weather <|message|><atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="get_weather"> <atem:parameter name="city"> Paris </atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls><|eom|> NVIDIA Nemotron 3 </think> <tool_call> <function= get_weather > <parameter=city> Paris </parameter> </function> </tool_call> Table 1. Model-specific inputs with the same expected GOLDEN output: get_weather({“city”:”Paris”}) Tutorial: Create a new parser Now you can create a parser for a model that frontend-crates doesn’t support yet. Ask your AI agent to read this post and work through the tutorial, starting with the prompt in step 1. Your model’s specification defines the grammar; the shared cases provide behaviors to test. You’ll need a frontend-crates checkout, Rust and Cargo, and the conformance dependencies. The parser exercise runs on a CPU using fixed test fixtures, so you don’t need a GPU. End-to-end testing also requires a working Dynamo runtime, discovery services, and hardware for your model. When you’re ready to test end-to-end, launch the tests with Dynamo runtime on the actual model and GPU(s). The workflow in Figure 2 starts with the model’s grammar, recovery rules, and reviewed GOLDEN expectations. The agent writes or fixes the parser, runs tests, and uses failures to guide the next change. If it proposes changing the expected behavior, review that decision before accepting it. Test your parser end to end with real models before claiming deployment support. Plan time to allocate a machine, load the model, initialize the runtime, and run your own test cases. Turn failures into unit tests for the agent, then rerun the end-to-end test to check the fix. Figure 2. Iterate with unit tests, then test with real models. Turn end-to-end failures into regression tests before continuing 1. Start with a prompt Give the agent this prompt: In the frontend-crates checkout, follow .agents/skills/tool-parser-generator/SKILL.md to create a v2 Unified parser for [MODEL_NAME]. Research its grammar and prepare the GOLDEN test set, adapting applicable UNIFIED.* cases. Pause for human review. After approval, implement, validate, and provide the local conformance report URL for human inspection. 2. Define the GOLDEN test set The GOLDEN test set defines the behavior your parser will be tested against. Use the prompt in step 1 to have the agent generate an initial test set in conformance/fixtures-unified-v2/families/<name>/inputs_and_golden.yaml , independently of parser results. Each case pairs an input with its expected output, called GOLDEN. If those expectations are wrong, the parser can pass the tests and still behave incorrectly. The following example pairs an input with its expected GOLDEN output. It omits request definitions, tools, initialization, and chunk settings; the existing nemotron_v3/inputs_and_golden.yaml shows the full format. family: nemotron_v3
cases: UNIFIED.tool_only.nemotron_v3: input: |- </think><tool_call> <function=get_weather> <parameter=city>Paris</parameter> </function></tool_call> golden: - kind: tool_call name: get_weather arguments: {city: Paris} Ask the agent for an adversarial review, then go through the set manually, case by case. The initial test set may contain errors because expected behavior depends on context the agent may not have.

item.title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
item.abstract: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API , a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency , and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI . It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1 . Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator , without /v1 . Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: You cannot pick a deployment yourself. Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. Routing is in preview. You set model to perplexity/auto and pass a routing object. It holds a default_model and 1 to 5 routes , each with a name, description and model. A decision model reads the conversation and route descriptions. It never sees route names or model IDs. If nothing matches, or the decision model fails or times out, the default model answers. So do media inputs. Response headers report the result: x-perplexity-autoroute-outcome , -route and -confidence . The default policy sends traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, with simple requests going to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity also lists built-in Lower cost, Balanced and Higher quality profiles, plus an Auto effort preview. Perplexity tested this on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 , run in Claude Code. Anthropic documents that Claude Fable 5.2 safeguards can block benign security and life sciences work. The routes covered security , biology and after_refusal requests. That is +3 tasks, at a higher estimated cost per task. Perplexity calls it an adjusted comparison; results vary by workload. Each request is billed at the answering model’s published per-token rate. Failover to another provider does not change the rate. Perplexity says there is no additional platform fee on top of credits . For example, perplexity/glm-5.3 lists $1.4 input, $4.4 output and $0.26 cache read per 1M tokens . Usage draws from prepaid Perplexity API credits, also purchasable through AWS Marketplace. item.title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
item.abstract: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace , so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer . Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill. To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID. An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace , agents can only buy the products it allows. In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account. Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was announced about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints. The agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost. In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use. Figure 2: End-to-end flow of the sample solution using a Strands agent 1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts. 2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected. 3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the ProcessPayment API with the payment type AWS_BILLING_X402 . If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged. 4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass. 5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and shows up in their AWS bill monthly. To create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce . AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details. The open-source GitHub sample in the agentcore-samples repository runs through a demo of the new functionality. It can help you configure AgentCore payments for AWS Marketplace, connect Tavily, run the agent, and inspect the transaction. You can refer to the documentation for more details. setup_aws_billing.py creates a payment manager with an AWS Billing connector, plus the AWS Marketplace service-linked role and three separate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. The session role can set budgets but can’t pay. Meanwhile the agent role can pay but can’t create sessions, so the agent has no way to raise its own budget. setup_gateway.py creates an AgentCore Gateway with the AWS Marketplace connector and gives the agent role the appropriate permissions to use it. The gateway’s role is limited to three read-only AWS Marketplace actions. If you choose to skip this step, you can instead set SELLER_URL in the environment variables to the seller’s endpoint, and the agent will pay that URL only rather than using AgentCore Gateway discovery. The script creates a payment session as the session role and then runs the agent as the agent role. By default the session budget is $0.05 and the per-request cap is $0.02. The agent searches, looks at listings, gets an endpoint, and pays once. In this test run against a $0.01 seller, it compared two listings before buying: When the run finishes, the sample will print the payment with its amount, AWS Marketplace product ID, and processPaymentId . The AWS Marketplace meters charges asynchronously, so the Tavily line item takes a moment to appear on your bill. Agent purchases will also show up in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Run cleanup.

item.title: Genie ZeroOps, now in public beta: An autonomous agent that fixes data pipelines, with lessons from 80,000 customer issues
item.abstract: In June we introduced Genie ZeroOps , an autonomous agent that detects, investigates, and resolves data pipeline issues, such as upstream schema changes or data quality anomalies. Based on extensive private preview testing with hundreds of customers, we’ve added new features to help data teams triage issues faster - including inbox sharing, notifications, one-click PR creation, and the ability to add custom business instructions to follow specific company workflows. Today, Genie ZeroOps is available in Public Beta, and your workspace admin can turn it on from the workspace Previews page. Data engineering teams are underwater, managing many thousands of pipelines a day. Some pipeline failures are easy to find and fix - a job fails, a pipeline update errors out, and someone gets paged. Others are silent - a table stops updating, or last night's load arrives with half its usual rows, and nobody notices until a dashboard shows the wrong number. Either way, the work that follows typically looks the same: a notification is sent, an engineer spends the next few hours manually investigating logs, upstream tables, and related assets, and finally a PR gets generated with the fix. Genie ZeroOps automates this entire manual workflow while maintaining security, governance, and recommendation quality, specifically guiding teams from initial issue alert to a pull request across five core steps: During the limited private preview, ZeroOps observed over 80,000 real customer issues across hundreds of companies, highlighting just how painful pipeline maintenance has become. We found that over half of issues require organization-specific knowledge to properly triage, rank, and resolve, which speaks to the fundamental need for custom context. Through this feedback, we identified and built several critical features every team needs to succeed with ZeroOps: During our private preview, we spoke with customers who were prototyping internal AI triage tools. We learned that while building a simple prototype has become easier, scaling automated triage across production environments introduces complex operational challenges that compound over time: Genie ZeroOps handles these complexities natively - leveraging direct access to your Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage to resolve issues with full context. Try ZeroOps out for yourself! Have a workspace admin enable the ZeroOps feature. Then find the ZeroOps banner on the top of the pipelines page: Read the documentation here for more details on how to get started. If your team needs help onboarding ZeroOps to production, reach out to your account team to inquire about any workshops that we offer. item.title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization
item.abstract: Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a company’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge. Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) , so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI. Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inherently limits the representation power of the fine-tuned model. As tasks grow more complex and datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples, LoRA hits an accuracy plateau where increasing rank (and thus trainable parameters) fails to bridge the accuracy gap with standard fine-tuning. This plateau reveals that the performance gap isn’t simply because of fewer parameters. It’s caused by rank deficiency itself. The low-rank update can’t capture the full complexity of the weight changes needed for deep task adaptation. However, for complex tasks and domains where large, good-quality datasets exist, full-rank fine-tuning excels by updating model parameters simultaneously. FFT modifies the model’s weight matrix uniformly, using the full representational capacity of the model’s weight matrices rather than restricting updates to a small subspace, and without introducing the abrupt, localized distortions characteristic of low-rank methods. The result is stronger model convergence, better activation alignment across model layers, and a model that faithfully captures both the target task distribution and the richness of its pre-trained knowledge. FFT’s quality advantage grows with dataset scale: at 100K+ training examples, FFT achieved 90.0 percent on LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness across code generation tasks, as shown in the following chart. Figure 1: LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness by training method as training data scales to 100K+ examples Furthermore, the following radar chart provides a holistic view: the base model (inner polygon) shows consistently low scores across all axes. LoRA (middle polygon) shows strong, balanced improvement. FFT (outer polygon) extends further on every dimension, with particularly pronounced leads on BLEU and ROUGE-2 scores. This multi-dimensional quality lead confirms that it isn’t a metric-specific artifact but a fundamental advantage of full-rank optimization. Figure 2: Radar chart comparing the base model, LoRA, and FFT across quality dimensions The details of how we arrived at these results, the coding datasets used for model customization, and the experimentation process are explained in detail in the following sections. In this post we used the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) technique on a Qwen3-4B base model offered within Amazon SageMaker AI Studio and performed all the fine-tuning experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization across LoRA and FFT training methods. Within each experiment, both methods received the same prompts, targets, and evaluation code. For all the experimentation, we fine-tuned the Qwen3-4B base model on the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset, a curated corpus of 110,000 coding instruction-response pairs spanning algorithm design, debugging, data structures, and systems programming. We applied a 90/5/5 split to the dataset: 99,000 records for training, 5,500 for validation to monitor convergence and training loss during the customization job, and 5,500 reserved as a held-out test set for unbiased evaluation of the final model, as registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets and shown in the following figure. Figure 3: The 110K instruction-pair dataset registered in SageMaker AI dataset assets All the model customization experiments in this post were performed on Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization. Serverless Model Customization on SageMaker AI lets data scientists and machine learning (ML) engineers focus on model fine-tuning without managing infrastructure or GPU capacity planning. You specify the base model, dataset, and hyperparameters, and the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically in a serverless fashion. The following code snippet shows one such experiment for launching a Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) job on Serverless Model Customization using the SageMaker Python SDK. The code triggers a serverless model customization job, shown in the following screenshot, with training performance metrics tracked in the job and viewable in the linked MLflow app. Figure 4: Serverless model customization job with training metrics tracked in MLflow Switching from Full Fine-Tuning to LoRA requires only one change: set TrainingType.FULL to TrainingType.LORA . The rest of the code remains identical: We tested the resulting customized models across three diverse evaluation methods built into SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization: LLM-as-Judge, PRIMECODE, and MMLU, shown in the following image. Each targets a different dimension of model quality: semantic correctness, code generation fidelity, and general knowledge retention. Together they provide a comprehensive picture of the model customization quality. Figure 5: The three built-in evaluation methods in SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization The LLM-as-Judge metric uses a frontier model (in this post, Amazon Nova Pro) as an automated evaluator that reads the model’s generated code alongside the original prompt and judges whether the solution is logically correct. On serverless model customization you can evaluate both the customized model alongside the base model, as shown in the following figure. Figure 6: LLM-as-Judge evaluation comparing the customized model and the base model PRIMECODE is a custom scorer evaluation that measures how closely the model’s generated code matches reference solutions using deterministic text-similarity metrics: BLEU (n-gram precision), ROUGE-1/2/L (recall-oriented overlap), and F1 (precision-recall balance). These metrics are fully reproducible, making them ideal for controlled ablation studies.

item.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
item.abstract: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073 . It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc). When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI. We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead. You can get started with `npm create factory`. It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!  https://factory.mastra.ai   https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory
