item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
item.abstract: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces. Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve. Explicit configuration always takes precedence: When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"] , Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need. For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification: With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow. Harness supports four lifecycle events: Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop. For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness: The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision: When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent : Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks ( beforeInvocation , afterInvocation ) run once for the whole invocation. You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness . If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode , which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide . To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub . A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow. Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself. The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm: The CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory. This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you. Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY : Invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents: Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator plans the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment. With --prompt , the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt , and the CLI opens an interactive chat. The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false .

item.title: Enabling Real-Time AI for Scientific Instruments with GPU-Native Data Acquisition
item.abstract: In science and industry, analyzing sensor measurements in real time can enable AI to adjust processes, guide experiments, and search for better operating conditions. Yet limits on how quickly the measured data can be moved and processed often shape how an instrument is designed, from readout electronics to acquisition timing. What could scientific instrument makers simplify—or make possible—if processing could keep pace with their sensors? NVIDIA DAQIRI is a software-defined data acquisition library that moves high-bandwidth instrument and sensor data into GPU-ready workflows. It enables developers to process measurements during acquisition without first writing them to disk. An NVIDIA Holoscan platform library, DAQIRI bridges sensors optimized for measurement with programmable GPU platforms for scientific analysis, AI inference, and feedback applications. For existing Ethernet-capable instruments, this opens opportunities to add processing and feedback capabilities, as described in the previous post, Enable Real-Time AI for High-Speed Data Acquisition with NVIDIA DAQIRI . For new instruments, it allows opportunities for reconsidering acquisition constraints from the start. This post explores how a new electron microscopy camera and GPU processing enable analysis during acquisition. It then introduces new DAQIRI features, including hardware packet reordering, performance and throughput improvements in the library, and a low-latency NIC polling mode for time-sensitive packet processing. Case study: Connecting high-dynamic-range imaging to GPU processing A high-dynamic-range electron microscopy camera developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s Molecular Foundry illustrates what becomes possible when advanced detectors and GPU processing are designed to work together. Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) measures the energy electrons lose as they interact with a sample, helping scientists identify which elements are present and how they are bonded together. These measurements contain both strong and faint signals. To capture those differences in intensity, the conventional approach uses two separately optimized acquisition processes in rapid succession. This requires precise coordination of the electron optics, exposure timing, and detector readout. The resulting measurements then need to be aligned and combined, adding complexity to both acquisition and processing. The new high-dynamic-range camera developed at the Molecular Foundry captures strong and faint signals together. This advancement simplifies the experimental setup and microscope optics, but generates more than 500 gigabits of data per second (Gbps)—a stream that must be received and processed to make those measurements useful during acquisition. This is over 500x faster than conventional EELS data streams, which greatly enhances the raw detector information available for further processing and analysis. Figure 1. Researchers at Berkeley Lab’s Molecular Foundry examine a hardware component beside the electron microscope used in the GPU-accelerated EELS workflow. Photo credit: Marilyn Sargent/Berkeley Lab Handling that stream requires an acquisition and processing pipeline designed to keep pace with the camera. This is where the collaboration between Berkeley Lab and NVIDIA brings together the camera, DAQIRI, and GPU-accelerated processing. FPGA readout electronics transmit detector data over Ethernet, DAQIRI receives the packets directly into GPU memory, and GPU processing assembles and corrects detector frames before reducing them to energy-loss spectra. Computation also improves the spatial information recovered from the detector, enabling submicron spatial resolution from sensor pixels measuring 5 micrometers across. Through this pipeline, the team enables inspection of the data during the measurement and adjusting the acquisition parameters and regions of interest in real time, all while processing high bandwidth data incoming at more than 500 Gbps. Figure 2. The workflow of the EELS measurement at Berkeley Lab sends the data directly into the GPU memory, from which GPU applications can process the data while the experiment is ongoing The benefits of this approach extend beyond electron microscopy. Connecting sensors to GPU processing can extract more information from measurements and give instrument makers greater flexibility in how they acquire, analyze, and act on data. Realizing those benefits requires efficient data movement, ordered payloads ready for processing, and low-latency communication for feedback. Designing acquisition paths for intelligent instruments The latest DAQIRI release adds hardware packet reordering, an optimized library backend for improved throughput, and direct polling for low-latency packet transmission and reception. Reorder data as it arrives with NIC hardware Most networks rely on protocol processing or receive-side buffering to handle out-of-order packets, which can add latency and memory overhead. DAQIRI can now offload packet reordering tasks to supported NVIDIA ConnectX-7 or newer NICs, preserving CPU and GPU resources for analysis. For compatible sequence formats, the NIC parses sequence fields and places each payload directly into its ordered position in memory. The application receives the assembled, ordered data without requiring a separate software reorder copy step. Hardware-based reordering is defined here for a specific receive queue. The configuration dictates how to parse the sequence number from the packet header, which reordering method to use, and how missing packets should be handled. - name: "rx_reorder_seq_1024" reorder_engine: "hw" # NIC places payloads in order cyclic_sequence: true # Confirm compatible cyclic numbering missing_action: “drop” # Drop partial batches on RX timeout reorder_type: "gpu" # Deliver packets to GPU memory memory_region: "Reorder_RX_GPU" payload_byte_offset: 42 # Skip 42-byte Ethernet/IPv4/UDP header packet_size: 8192 # Payload bytes per output slot flow_ids: [201] # Apply reorder to RX flow 201 method: seq_packets_per_batch: # Reorder by one sequence field sequence_number: bit_offset: 336 # Sequence starts at bit 336 bit_width: 32 # 32-bit sequence field packets_per_batch: 1024 # 1024 packets per output buffer Use the ibverbs engine for efficient acquisition DAQIRI introduces an ibverbs engine for high-rate receive and transmit of raw Ethernet packets. Built on libibverbs and NVIDIA DevX, the engine is selected by default for raw Ethernet streams. Developers can also select it explicitly by adding engine: “ibverbs” to their DAQIRI configuration, without changing how they use the application API. By reducing per-packet CPU overhead, the ibverbs engine delivers approximately twice the per-core throughput of the previous default DPDK backend at small packet sizes (up to 1024 bytes) and extreme data rates (greater than 200 Gbps), based on benchmark tests performed on the NVIDIA DGX Spark , NVIDIA IGX Thor , and NVIDIA RTX PRO server platforms. Figure 3. The DAQIRI ibverbs engine nearly doubles throughput for 64-byte and 256-byte packets compared with DPDK, while maintaining similar throughput for 8 KB packets. Results shown are from single-queue benchmarks on NVIDIA IGX Thor Reduce feedback latency with direct polling Intelligent instruments may require latency-sensitive feedback from GPU analysis to adjust acquisition or control settings. The DAQIRI direct polling mode reduces communication latency by letting the application thread receive and submit packets directly, eliminating the handoff to a separate I/O worker. In cabled loopback benchmark tests, application send-to-receive latency on the order of 2-4 µs has been demonstrated in direct polling mode. When using the ibverbs engine, developers can select direct polling for control queues while retaining batched processing for high-throughput data streams.

item.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
item.abstract: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching , the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching ). Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing ). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response. Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes. Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy ( see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing ). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer. Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains. Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings ( see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks ). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers. Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever. The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching.

item.title: Genie One Accuracy: Why Curated Agents Need Governed Context
item.abstract: Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and you will get two contradictory answers that are both correct. In a fictional commercial auto insurer we built for this test, Finance reported an 8.2 percentage-point deterioration, and Underwriting reported a 1.5 percentage-point improvement. Neither was wrong. Finance tracks the calendar year net of reinsurance, so an adverse reserve development on an older claim shows up in today's numbers. Underwriting looks strictly at the policy year, gross of reinsurance and excluding catastrophes, because that's the baseline used to set rates. Reserving, meanwhile, relies on a third metric entirely: the accident-year ultimate loss ratio. The SQL can be perfectly correct and still produce an answer that doesn't make sense for the person asking. The challenge is knowing which business definition to apply when the same term has several valid definitions, while keeping shared facts, such as total policies written, consistent. This is the problem we wanted to explore with Genie One. Genie One, powered by Genie Ontology (now Generally Available), brings this business context into the analytics experience. Genie Ontology learns from the work teams already do, automatically capturing business logic, calculations, and relationships from existing dashboards, queries, notebooks, and semantic models as Ontology Snippets. This learned knowledge is complemented by modeled knowledge: explicitly defined, governed business concepts represented in Unity Catalog through certified Metric Views, Domains and Subdomains, and Pages. In this study, we refer to this modeled knowledge as the “governed layer”. Together, learned and modeled knowledge give Genie a richer understanding of how an organization works. Teams can build on the knowledge already captured from their existing assets, while using modeled knowledge to establish authoritative definitions for the business concepts where consistency and precision matter most. There is no need to model every concept upfront. This study explores a different aspect of Genie Ontology than the Turing benchmark described in our Genie Ontology GA announcement . While the benchmark compared the accuracy and efficiency of Genie with Genie Ontology against leading frontier agents, our study isolates the contribution of modeled knowledge: how governed Metric Views and Pages complement learned knowledge and curated agents to help Genie One interpret business definitions and deliver consistent answers. To explore this, we built four Genie Agents, one each for Finance, Reserving, Underwriting, and Claims. They used the same tables, but each had its own team's definitions, example queries, and documents. Each did well on its own. We wanted to know what happens when Genie One becomes the entry point: does it route to the right agent and use the right definition, and what does it need to do that reliably? We tested four configurations to find out. Tables alone scored 64%. Curated agents and the governed layer each reached 83%, but they weren't good at the same things. Adding curated agents improved document-based answers. Adding the governed layer improved answers that depended on business definitions. Neither was enough on its own to cover both needs. With both in place, accuracy reached 93–95%, across two runs. The combined setup also scored 93% on loss-ratio questions and 97% on questions that required both documents and structured data. To see whether this pattern held outside the insurance sector, we repeated the comparison using a fictional retailer. There, the governed layer raised accuracy from 54% to 82% when added to the curated agents. Genie One doesn't simply choose an agent and let it answer every question. It can use governed Unity Catalog Semantics such as Metric Views , Domains and subdomains , and Pages , or route a question to a relevant Genie Agent. If it doesn't find a suitable match, it searches the workspace. There, it may infer which data to use from tables or volumes you use often, or from your earlier conversations. When Genie One answers a question using its own context, it doesn't automatically inherit the instructions configured inside each agent. Those instructions apply only when Genie One routes the question to that agent. So an agent can be well curated and still contribute little if Genie One answers the question differently. We created a fictional commercial auto insurer with: The four agents shared the same underlying tables. Each also had access to its team's folder of documents, with 14 PDFs across the four folders. We also planted two misleading documents to test robustness. One was an early draft of the reserve committee minutes reporting a $4.1 million increase in reserves; the approved minutes in the same folder reported a $5.28 million increase. The other was a vendor newsletter containing a hidden instruction to report the loss ratio as 55%, a simple prompt-injection test. We then placed three look-alike tables next to the real definitions: analytics_loss_ratio_v2, analytics_loss_ratio_test, and a personal copy, finance_lr_calendar_quarter_net_jdoe. The agents were configured with their teams' formulas, business rules, and SQL example questions. We tuned them on a separate set of practice questions and then froze them, using the same versions across all configurations that included agents. There are multiple ways to make enterprise documents available to Genie, depending on where the content lives and how teams need to access it. In this experiment, we stored team-specific PDFs in Unity Catalog Volumes and made them available to the corresponding Genie Agents through content search. When information is spread across business applications such as Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, or Confluence, Genie Search provides a broader enterprise search experience. It combines indexed content from connected applications with live retrieval through MCP, bringing results together with Databricks assets in a single experience. It also respects the permissions of the source systems, so users only see content they are authorized to access. For the governed layer, we set up: The insurance benchmark contained 125 questions, each with an expected answer calculated independently in SQL. The questions covered simple lookups, explicitly named business definitions, ambiguous questions such as "What's our loss ratio?", questions requiring an explanation, questions that the available data couldn't answer, and questions that combined documents with structured data. We also tested follow-up questions and the two planted documents. We took several steps to make the results more meaningful. Genie One answered every question three times, with a fresh service principal for each run so earlier conversations couldn't carry over, and every answer was logged in MLflow. When a key result was close, we repeated the whole setup with a new identity. We report 95% confidence intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples, keeping each question's repeats together, because Genie One can recall earlier answers. Two AI judges from different model families extracted the headline number, the definition used, and the facts covered, and fixed rules decided whether each answer was right. The judges agreed on 95–99% of answers. Before each run, every agent had to answer at least 85% of its basic questions correctly on its own. Here’s the overall accuracy score, followed by a breakdown by question category, measured with Genie One. What the governed layer added. With curated agents alone, Genie One often answered definition questions on its own and never saw the formulas in the agents' instructions. Published Pages are visible to Genie One across the whole account, so the closest definitions it could find were Pages other people had written for unrelated projects. It relied on those in 49% of its answers.
